Key Features: Basic "retrieve-read" framework using query encoding, document retrieval (often via TF-IDF, BM25, or simple vector search), and response generation.
Strengths: Simple and cost-effective to deploy; reduces hallucinations compared to standalone LLMs; requires no fine-tuning.
Limitations: Struggles with retrieval precision; prone to noise, redundancy, and fragmented outputs; limited handling of multi-intent or complex queries.
Typical Use Cases: Basic Q&A, simple knowledge retrieval, quick prototypes, and customer support chatbots for repetitive questions.

Key Features: Introduces pre-retrieval (query rewriting, expansion) and post-retrieval (reranking, context compression, sliding window chunking) optimizations.
Strengths: Higher precision and contextual relevance; mitigates irrelevant context; better handles domain-specific nuances and semantic alignment.
Limitations: Higher computational overhead and latency; more complex to implement and maintain; resource-intensive preprocessing.
Typical Use Cases: Research synthesis, professional customer tools, and production-grade applications requiring moderate complexity.

Key Features: Flexible, plug-and-play architecture with specialized functional modules (search, memory, routing, fusion) and task adapters; supports iterative/recursive retrieval.
Strengths: Highly scalable and customizable; allows independent debugging of components; handles multi-source retrieval and multi-turn interactions.
Limitations: Increased architectural complexity; requires sophisticated orchestration; higher costs due to multiple LLM calls and parallel processing.
Typical Use Cases: Enterprise workflows, complex domain-specific management (legal, healthcare, finance), and multi-domain financial analytics.

Key Features: Uses knowledge graphs (entities/edges) as the retrieval substrate; involves entity extraction, community detection (Leiden), and community summarization.
Strengths: Superior multi-hop reasoning; high explainability; triples accuracy in enterprise settings; excels at global/exploratory questions and thematic analysis.
Limitations: Indexing is 100-1000x more expensive than vector RAG; requires complex schema design; slower query times due to graph traversal.
Typical Use Cases: Medical research (Alzheimer's), legal discovery, fraud detection, and query-focused summarization over large narrative datasets.

Key Features: Modeled as a sequential decision-making system (POMDP) where autonomous agents coordinate planning, reflection, tool use, and multi-agent collaboration.
Strengths: Unparalleled flexibility; handles multi-step reasoning and dynamic real-time changes; self-improving through feedback loops and autonomous correction.
Limitations: High resource/computational overhead; risk of compounding hallucinations across iterations; complex coordination and potential for high latency.
Typical Use Cases: Autonomous enterprise assistants, complex research and development, and long-horizon workflows like software engineering.
